questions.question: A researcher reports all findings, including those that contradict the original expectations. This practice primarily reflects which characteristic of good research? A. Objectivity B. Flexibility C. Generalizability D. Economical use of resources
questions.solution_html:
• A literature review is a systematic survey and critical evaluation of existing research related to a problem. It
  • contributes throughout research, beginning when a question is first considered. Establishes background/existing
  • knowledge; reveals gaps and contradictions; clarifies problems, objectives and hypotheses; builds
  • theoretical/conceptual frameworks; guides variables, design, sampling, tools and statistics; avoids unnecessary
  • duplication; strengthens originality/credibility; enables comparison of new and previous findings. Primary sources
  • Original peer-reviewed research articles, theses/dissertations, conference papers, patents, official research reports
  • and raw datasets provide first-hand evidence and methodological detail. Secondary sources: Textbooks, review
  • articles, meta-analyses, handbooks, encyclopedias and edited books summarize or interpret original work.
  • Tertiary/locating resources: Library catalogues, bibliographies, indexes, abstracts and databases/search tools
  • Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, JSTOR and ERIC. Other sources: Government/census
  • publications, policy documents, annual reports, newspapers, professional association publications and grey
  • literature, including working papers and conference proceedings.
  • Review methods: Narrative/traditional: Broad, flexible contextual overview, less structured. Systematic
  • Predefined protocol, explicit searches, inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality appraisal and synthesis reduce bias.
  • Scoping: Maps the extent/nature of broad or emerging literature, concepts and gaps. Meta-analysis: Statistically
  • combines comparable quantitative results into an overall estimate. Meta-synthesis: Integrates qualitative findings.
  • Theoretical: Examines/compares theories. Critical: Evaluates strengths, weaknesses and assumptions. Procedure
  • Define topic; select keywords; search databases; screen relevance/quality; organize thematically or chronologically;
  • compare studies, identify gaps and synthesize critically; cite accurately to avoid plagiarism.

questions.question: A clearly defined research problem helps the researcher work out the a). Research design b). Research budget only c). Publication format d). Reference list
questions.solution_html:
• A sample is a smaller representation selected from a population according to a plan. A sample-based measure is
  • a statistic. Sampling error is the chance discrepancy between a sample statistic (e.g., sample mean) and the
  • population parameter because only a subset is studied.
  • Reduction: (1) Increase sample size to improve precision and reduce variance. (2) Use probability sampling, such
  • as simple random, stratified or systematic sampling: every member has a known, non-zero selection probability
  • limiting subjective selection and allowing sampling-error estimation. (3) Use stratified random sampling: divide
  • heterogeneous populations into homogeneous strata (age, income, education), then sample randomly within strata to
  • ensure subgroup representation. (4) Optimize design and allocation through appropriate
  • proportional/disproportionate allocation and oversampling small or highly variable groups when required.

• Probability and non-probability sampling
  • Probability: Random selection gives every member a known, non-zero inclusion chance. It supports sampling-error
  • estimation, inferential statistics, hypothesis testing and population estimation. Types: simple random, stratified
  • cluster. Example: randomly choosing 1,000 IDs from 10,000 university students gives each a 1-in-10 chance.

  • Selection bias limits statistical generalization, but it suits qualitative/exploratory work, low budgets and hidden

questions.question: A researcher categorizes participants according to their preferred mode of transportation: bus, train, bicycle, or car. Which measurement scale is being used? A. Nominal B. Ordinal C. Interval D. Ratio
questions.solution_html:
• Reliability and validity are the two essential qualities of any data-collection tool, such as a questionnaire, interview
  • schedule, test, rating scale, checklist, or observation schedule. Reliability means the consistency, stability, and
  • dependability of a tool; a reliable tool produces similar results when used repeatedly under similar conditions, with
  • the same respondents, or by diff erent trained observers. Validity means the accuracy or truthfulness of a tool; it
  • measures whether the instrument actually measures the concept it claims to measure. Both are necessary because
  • unreliable or invalid tools produce inaccurate data, leading t o wrong analysis, interpretation, and conclusions.
  • Reliability is important because it reduces random errors and increases confidence in the collected data. A reliable
  • questionnaire or test gives nearly the same score when administered again after a short interval, when scored by
  • different examiners, or when its items consistently measure the same characteristic. The major types are test –retest
  • reliability (stability of scores over
  • time), inter-rater reliability (agreement between observers or scorers), int ernal consistency reliability (consistency
  • among items of a scale), and parallel -form reliability (equivalence of two versions of the same tool). Reliability is
  • commonly tested through the test–retest method, split -half method, Cronbach’s alpha, and correl ation
  • coefficients. It is
  • especially important in surveys, psychological testing, experiments, and observation because it makes results
  • replicable and strengthens the scientific value of the study. Validity is important because it ensures that the tool
  • measures the intended variable rather than some unrelated characteristic. For example, a test designed to measure
  • mathematical
  • ability is valid only if it genuinely measures mathematical ability and not merely language skill or memory. The main
  • types are face validity (whether the tool appears appropriate), content validity (whether items cover all aspects of the
  • concept), construct validity (whether the tool measures the underlying theoretical construct), and criterion validity
  • (whether the tool’s results agree with an established measure or predict a future outcome). Validity can be established
  • through expert judgement, pilot testing, comparison with standardized instruments, correlation analysis, and
  • factor analysis. A tool may be reliable without being valid for example, a weighing machine may consistently show
  • an incorrect weight but a valid tool must also be reliable. Thus, reliability and validity together ensure accuracy
  • consistency, credibility, and generalizability of research findings, making them indispensable in the construction and
  • use of data-collection instruments.
questions.source_exam: Dynamics Of Research In Psychology
questions.final_answer: use of data-collection instruments.

• Exploratory and descriptive research designs
  • A research design is the conceptual structure within which research is conducted. Exploratory design addresses
  • poorly defined or little-understood problems. As Kothari emphasizes, it discovers ideas/insights and clarifies
  • problems or hypotheses. It is flexible, open and discovery-oriented; methods include literature review, experience
  • surveys/expert interviews and insight-stimulating cases. It asks, “What is going on here?”
  • Descriptive design documents existing characteristics, functioning or prevalence without manipulating variables. It
  • is structured and pre-planned to reduce bias and improve reliability, using surveys, standardized questionnaires
  • observation schedules and systematic sampling. It asks, “What are the characteristics or prevalence?” Exploratory
  • research generates hypotheses; descriptive research measures existing conditions and establishes facts.

  • the same respondents, or by diff erent trained observers. Validity means the accuracy or truthfulness of a tool; it
  • measures whether the instrument actually measures the concept it claims to measure. Both are necessary because
  • unreliable or invalid tools produce inaccurate data, leading t o wrong analysis, interpretation, and conclusions.
  • Reliability is important because it reduces random errors and increases confidence in the collected data. A reliable
  • questionnaire or test gives nearly the same score when administered again after a short interval, when scored by
  • different examiners, or when its items consistently measure the same characteristic. The major types are test –retest
  • reliability (stability of scores over
  • time), inter-rater reliability (agreement between observers or scorers), int ernal consistency reliability (consistency
  • among items of a scale), and parallel -form reliability (equivalence of two versions of the same tool). Reliability is
  • commonly tested through the test–retest method, split -half method, Cronbach’s alpha, and correl ation
  • coefficients. It is
  • especially important in surveys, psychological testing, experiments, and observation because it makes results
  • replicable and strengthens the scientific value of the study. Validity is important because it ensures that the tool
  • measures the intended variable rather than some unrelated characteristic. For example, a test designed to measure
  • mathematical
  • ability is valid only if it genuinely measures mathematical ability and not merely language skill or memory. The main
  • types are face validity (whether the tool appears appropriate), content validity (whether items cover all aspects of the
  • concept), construct validity (whether the tool measures the underlying theoretical construct), and criterion validity
  • (whether the tool’s results agree with an established measure or predict a future outcome). Validity can be established
  • through expert judgement, pilot testing, comparison with standardized instruments, correlation analysis, and
  • factor analysis. A tool may be reliable without being valid for example, a weighing machine may consistently show
  • an incorrect weight but a valid tool must also be reliable. Thus, reliability and validity together ensure accuracy
  • consistency, credibility, and generalizability of research findings, making them indispensable in the construction and
  • use of data-collection instruments.
